newsitem.title: USA: Marine general nominated to head U.S. forces in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Marine general nominated to head U.S. forces in Gulf.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has nominated Marine Lt. Gen. Anthony Zinni to head the key U.S. Central Command with responsibility for American troops in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf, the Pentagon said on Thursday.

Zinni, 54, must be confirmed by the Senate to replace Army Gen. Binford Peay, 57, who has headed the Central Command from its headquarters at MacDill Air Force Base in Tampa, Florida, for three years.

The post is seen as one of the most challenging in the U.S. military, with responsibility for an area including Iraq and Iran, especially after two terrorist car bomb attacks in Saudi Arabia since 1995 that have killed 24 American troops.
Zinni, a decorated Vietnam War veteran who would become a full general, is a 32-year military veteran and is currently deputy commander of the Central Command under Peay.
"He has had experience both as a warrior and as a peacekeeper and I think he is superbly well-qualified for this job,"," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.
Zinni served in the international military peacekeeping and humanitarian effort in Somalia in 1992 and 1993.
The elevation of Zinni to the Tampa job would continue a tradition of alternating the leadership of the Central Command between Army and Marine Corps generals.
"Should he be confirmed by the Senate, which we expect, he will take over in the summer," Bacon said.
Peay is scheduled to step down from his post in August after serving more than 34 years years in the military. He has not announced his plans after leaving the job.

Pentagon investigators earlier criticised U.S. military officials because they allegedly were not prepared for the two huge Saudi blasts -- one last June 25 at Dhahran that killed 19 Americans and one the previous November at Riyadh that killed five Americans.

The White House and Pentagon have stressed U.S. determination to protect the security of more than 6,000 U.S. troops stationed in Saudi Arabia. Most of those troops were moved to a remote, heavily guarded desert airbase last summer after the Dhahran bombing.

The Saudi government executed several Saudi dissidents which it said were responsible for the first blast. But there has been no determination of responsibility for last year's bombing, including whether or not it involved state-sponsored terrorism from any outside country.
